summary: For ages 8–9, build formal short (columnar) multiplication of 2- and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number ON TOP of the area/grid model so that 'carrying' is understood as regrouping place value, not a ritual. Estimate first to bound the answer, work partial products in columns with the carry recorded, then connect the compact answer back to the sum of the area sub-products. Core examples: 47×6=282 and 234×5=1170.
misconceptions: Treating carrying as a meaningless ritual and misplacing or forgetting the carried digit.
Multiplying only the ones and 'adding' the tens digit rather than multiplying it (place-value error): 47×6 giving 42+... wrong.
Aligning digits incorrectly or dropping a place, producing answers off by a factor of 10.
Not connecting the compact method to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.
Skipping estimation, so a wildly wrong magnitude goes unnoticed.

activities.title: Method bridge: area model beside the columns
steps: Estimate first by rounding a factor, e.g. for 234×5 use ≈200×5=1000 (or ≈50×6=300 for 47×6), and write the estimate down before calculating.
Draw an area/grid model splitting a factor by place value: for 234×5 make three sub-rectangles 200×5, 30×5 and 4×5; for 47×6 make 40×6 and 7×6.
Set out the same calculation in a short-multiplication column layout right next to the area model.

Work each partial product in the columns in lockstep with the matching sub-rectangle. For 234×5: 5×4=20 → write 0 in the ones and regroup 2 tens; 5×3=15, +2=17 → write 7 in the tens, regroup 1 hundred; 5×2=10, +1=11 → write 1 in the hundreds and 1 in the thousands, giving 1170.
Say aloud what each carried digit means, e.g. 'the little 2 is 2 regrouped tens'.
Add the area sub-products (1000+150+20=1170) and check they equal the columnar answer exactly.
Compare the finished answer against your estimate; if it is off by a factor of ten, look for a misaligned column.
activities.insight: The carried digits are the area model regrouped and folded into columns — multiply the digit first, THEN add the carry, keeping one digit per column.

activities.title: Make the carry visible with place-value counters
steps: Under the column headings, lay out the first factor with place-value counters as many times as the one-digit multiplier says (e.g. 6 groups of 47 for 47×6), so the counters show the whole product.
As you compute each partial product, physically move a regrouped ten (or hundred) one column to the left to represent the carried digit.
Match each counter move to the little digit you write above the next column.
Narrate: 'ten ones regroup into one ten, so the ten moves left.'
activities.insight: Carrying is the physical act of regrouping ten of one unit into one of the next place; the written carry records that move.

activities.title: Annotated worked example as a reference anchor
steps: Study a worked 234×5 with the area model above and the matching short-multiplication below.

For each column, read (or reveal) the explanation of the partial product and what its carry stands for, e.g. 'this is 2 regrouped tens' (from 5×4=20) and 'this is 1 regrouped hundred' (from 5×3=15, +2=17).
Match each area sub-rectangle to the column it feeds into.
activities.insight: Every column in the compact method has a home in the area model, and every carry names a specific regrouped place value.

activities.title: Consolidation and error-spotting checks
steps: Fill in the missing carry digit in a partly-worked 47×6.
Choose the best estimate for 234×5 from given options and justify the rounding.
Spot the error in a worked calculation where a carry was forgotten, and correct it.
Spot the error where someone added the carry before multiplying (e.g. did (4+4)×6=48 for 47×6) and explain the fix.
activities.insight: Short multiplication fails in specific, visible ways — a wrong magnitude, a missing carry, or a carry added before multiplying — and these can be diagnosed and corrected.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to set out and solve 47 × 6 and then 234 × 5 using the formal short-multiplication column method, watching how they record and carry. Then ask them to estimate 234 × 5 to check. Watch the carry handling and column alignment, not an explanation.
checkAnswer: 47 × 6 = 282 (6×7 = 42, write 2 carry 4; 6×4 = 24, +4 = 28). 234 × 5 = 1170 (5×4 = 20 write 0 carry 2; 5×3 = 15 +2 = 17 write 7 carry 1; 5×2 = 10 +1 = 11). Estimate 200×5 = 1000, so 1170 is reasonable. The teacher watches for correct carrying, adding the carry AFTER multiplying, and aligned columns.
